summary: This standards-track memo extends RMON to allow real-time quality-of-service monitoring of applications on end devices such as IP phones, pagers, messaging clients and mobile phones. It defines the framework, architecture, metrics and transport requirements, integrated with RMON through SNMP.

plainLanguage.summary: Phones and gadgets can report how good their calls and connections feel. This describes how they send those quality reports to a manager.

questions: what is a raqmon data source
subtitle: A framework for phones and other end devices to push real-time application quality reports to a collector, tied into RMON.

tldr.problem: Operators need to know what quality users actually get on IP phones, messaging clients and other end devices, but network-side monitoring cannot see device and application conditions.
tldr.mechanism: End devices act as RAQMON Data Sources and push reports of pre-defined QoS metrics to RAQMON Report Collectors. The collectors store the data in a MIB that extends RMON and is read over SNMP.
tldr.outcome: The framework defines the architecture, the basic metrics and the transport requirements, and leaves the exact PDU format and MIB to companion RFCs. It also asks for congestion-safe, secured transport.

facts.label: Safe UDP rate
facts.value: At most one PDU every two minutes

today: RFC 4710 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the framework document, with the PDU defined in RFC 4712 and the MIB in RFC 4711.

sections.title: Monitoring Quality at the End Device
sections.content:
IP phones, pagers, instant messaging clients, mobile phones and similar devices are now part of daily work. Enterprises and service providers need to ensure that end-user quality of service (QoS) goals are met. RAQMON extends the remote network monitoring (RMON) family (RFC 2819) so that end devices and applications can report QoS statistics in real time, and so that the data can be reached through SNMP.

The user experience depends on more than the network. For a VoIP call it includes call setup time, end-to-end delay, jitter, packet loss and codec, but also network protocols such as RSVP and DiffServ, and device resources such as CPU and memory. RAQMON therefore correlates three kinds of parameters: user, application and session parameters; IP end-device parameters; and transport network parameters.

The framework specifies a set of basic metrics sent as reports over existing protocols such as TCP or SNMP, requirements on the transport, and a MIB extension. Companion memos cover the PDU (RFC 4712) and the MIB (RFC 4711).
sections.plainLanguage: A good phone call depends on the network and on the phone itself. So the phone reports on both, not just on the wires in between.

sections.title: Data Sources, Collectors and the MIB
sections.content:
RAQMON has three functional components: the RAQMON Data Source (RDS), the RAQMON Report Collector (RRC) and the RAQMON MIB.

An RDS lives in an end device or application client and captures QoS attributes during communication sessions. It runs in the background, not in the data-forwarding path, and it uses a push model: it sends reports asynchronously, at a rate set by administrative policy. An RDS reports on simplex flows, so a report describes the session as perceived by the reporting device. Alice's phone and John's phone can see different delays on the same call. An RDS SHALL gather reports from multiple applications and send compound reports, and it MUST implement TCP transport and MAY implement SNMP transport.

An RDS must be configured with the interval between PDUs, which must avoid overflow of any parameter between transmissions, and the IP address and port of its RRC. Manual setup, TFTP scripts, DHCP, DNS or LDAP are mentioned as possibilities, and the RFC does not require any of them.

An RRC is a computationally resourceful network server that receives PDUs from many RDSs, analyzes them and stores the results. RRCs MUST support the mandatory TCP mapping from RFC 4712, MAY support SNMP notifications, MUST implement session timeouts to assume end of reporting, and MUST support the RAQMON-MIB module. Only RRCs should implement that MIB. Since RDSs can sit in different administrative domains, they may report to separate RRCs.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones are the students who fill out report cards. Collectors are the teachers who gather and file them. A shared notebook, the MIB, lets managers read the filed results.

sections.title: The RAQMON PDU and Information Model
sections.content:
RAQMON defines a set of basic metrics but does not require any minimum set. Instead, the information model is meant to be extended by vendors. As an example of an extension, the text points to the VoIP Metrics Report Block in RFC 3611.

The model is expressed as a conceptual RAQMON PDU, a common data format that sits where an application payload would, with different transports able to carry it. It has two parts. The BASIC part uses SMI Private Enterprise Code 0, which marks an IETF standard construct, and carries entries from the pre-defined list in Section 5. A report may contain just a subset, and static or rarely changing metrics are RECOMMENDED to be sent only at session start and then at large intervals. The Application part carries application-, vendor- and device-specific parameters, and the vendor's Private Enterprise Code indicates who owns the definition.

RDSs and RRCs are stateless for a whole reporting session, but the framework needs an end-of-reporting signal. An RDS MUST send a NULL PDU, a PDU with all NULL values.
sections.plainLanguage: The report card has a standard part everybody fills in and a free-form part for extra notes. When a student has nothing more to say, they hand in a blank card to mean the report is over.

sections.title: Transport Requirements and Congestion Safety
sections.content:
RAQMON leaves delivery to the underlying protocol. The transport SHOULD be lightweight enough for small devices, MUST be scalable, congestion safe as per RFC 2914, and secured with encryption and integrity, and SHOULD be NAT friendly as per RFC 3235. There is no retransmission in the framework, to keep it simple, but RAQMON MAY run over TCP when retransmission is needed. No framing mechanism is defined.

Over TCP, RAQMON is congestion safe. UDP has no feedback to pace a sender, and high fan-in (many RDSs reporting to one RRC) can cause congestion, so the RFC lists ways to use UDP safely:

  • Constant rate: for example one PDU per device every N seconds, with randomly jittered timers. At no more than one PDU every two minutes, a UDP implementation can be as congestion safe as one over TCP.
  • Single outstanding request: send, then wait for a response before sending again, with backed-off retransmissions. With SNMP, INFORM PDUs are RECOMMENDED and Traps are NOT RECOMMENDED. It is slow, so TCP, SCTP or a similar protocol SHOULD be used if more efficiency is needed.
  • Stay within the MTU: avoid fragmenting large PDUs, or split parameters across several PDUs that carry exactly the same NTP timestamp.
  • Bandwidth cap: it is RECOMMENDED that no more than 10% of network bandwidth be used for RDS/RRC reporting, whatever the transport.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone mails report cards at once, the post office jams. So you send them on a slow, steady schedule, one at a time, and never fill more than a small slice of the mailbag.

sections.title: The Basic Metrics
sections.content:
Section 5 defines the metrics in the BASIC part, mostly by pointing to existing IETF and ITU definitions. No device must report them all. Each metric says how often it should be sent. Measurement method is left to the implementer, but the collected data must match the semantics given, and IETF or ITU methods are RECOMMENDED where possible.

  • Identity and session: data source and receiver addresses (IPv4 or IPv6) and names, device ports (MUST be in the first PDU), setup date and time in NTP format, setup delay in milliseconds, session duration, and session setup status.
  • Delay: round-trip end-to-end delay (RFC 3550 for RTP, RFC 2681 otherwise), one-way delay (RFC 2679, which RAQMON SHOULD NOT derive by halving the round trip), and application delay inside the endpoint such as buffering, play-out and coding.
  • Jitter and variation: inter-arrival jitter as in RFC 3550, and IP packet delay variation as in RFC 3393.
  • Counters: application packets and octets sent and received, cumulative packet loss and loss fraction, and cumulative discards and discard fraction. Loss and discard are kept apart, and a late packet is counted as lost or discarded but not both.
  • Payload and priority: source and receiver payload types (for example value 8 for PCMA), Layer 2 priority and TOS/DSCP values.
  • Device state: CPU and memory utilization, where for multiple CPUs the maximum MUST be reported.
  • Application name and version: MUST be in the first PDU, and begins with RTP for RTP applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The report card has boxes for who called whom, how long the line took to connect, how late the words arrived, how many got lost, and whether the phone itself was tired out.

sections.title: Aggregation and Historical Data
sections.content:
RRCs have far more computing power than RDSs, so statistics are computed at the collector, not on the device. The RAQMON MIB provides only minimal aggregation: for selected metrics it keeps the mean, minimum and maximum over a communication session. For richer aggregation by protocol or application, the text points to the APM MIB (RFC 3729) and the TPM MIB (RFC 4150).

Because the data volume can be large, the RFC suggests ways to save space: publish data in the MIB only at the end of a session (on receipt of a NULL PDU), aggregate over time (for example one MIB entry per six data points when an RDS reports every 10 seconds and the RRC updates once a minute), or delete history under an administrative policy such as removing data older than 60 days.
sections.plainLanguage: The teacher does the maths. For each card, the teacher keeps the average, the best and the worst, and throws old cards away after a while.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The threats are those of the underlying layers plus attacks on the RAQMON payload: reading sensitive information in transit, modifying it (which can mix up sessions, enable denial of service, or falsify parameters and timestamps), malformed payloads aimed at an RRC, and disclosure of data carried in application PDUs.

The RFC says the framework needs authentication (the RRC can verify which RDS sent a PDU), privacy (reports identify the parties in a session) and protection against denial of service at the RRC. For the last one, an RDS sends the first report for a session only after the session has run for the five-second reporting interval, and holds shorter sessions until that interval expires.

RAQMON does not provide security itself. It relies on the transport protocol for end-to-end authentication, confidentiality, integrity, replay protection and key management, which avoids another mechanism. The drawbacks are that separating RAQMON sessions of one RDS-RRC pair needs separate transport instances, and that without transport security there is no RAQMON security.
sections.plainLanguage: Report cards can be read or changed on the way, or someone could flood the teacher with fake ones. So the mail needs a sealed, signed envelope, and phones wait a few seconds before reporting a call.
